notes.1: Generally a well answered question although a minority did not recognise or appreciate the definitions used.
notes.1a: (i) Generally correct although sometimes the lack of a systematic method often led to the omission of one factor, generally 18.
notes.1aii: Generally correct although a small minority gave common multiples as their answer rather than common factors.
notes.1b: Generally correct although a small minority gave answers of 5 squared, 6 squared, 7 squared or just 5,6,7, rather than the square numbers required. Other common errors included listing all even numbers or multiples of 5 within the given range.
notes.1c: This part proved more difficult with few candidates listing the prime factors of 56 before identifying p and q. A common error was p=8, q=7. Answers: (a)(i) 3,4,6,9,12,18 (ii) any two of 3,6,9,18 (b) 25,36,49 (c) p=2, q=7
notes.2a: Generally well answered with many candidates able to score full marks. However incomplete solutions were also common although the first method mark for calculating 18 or 88 was often attained. A common error was an answer of 27 coming from the incorrect working of 18 ÷100 x 150.
notes.2b: This standard ratio question was generally well answered. A small minority were unable to complete the first method line of 15+7+11=33.
notes.2c: This part caused more difficulties in the setting up of the fraction to be simplified. 11/2 was a common incorrect answer.
notes.2d: The majority of candidates correctly found the initial 8% but a significant number then failed to add it on as an increase. Few candidates used the alternative single method of 108÷100x150. Answers: (a) 12 (b) 60 (c) 2/11 (d) 162
notes.3: Throughout this question the conversion of minutes to fractions of hours caused initial problems and often led to incorrect answers following the application of the speed/distance/time formulae. This usually involved the incorrect use of 100.
notes.3a: Poorly answered with common errors being 8/15, 8/0.15 or 8/15 x100. The more successful responses came from using “15 minute is ¼ hour” leading to working of 8x4=32.
notes.3bii: As part (a) with common errors being 12/36 x100 and 36/12, but the more successful using the basic approach of “1/3 of an hour is 20 mins”.
notes.3iii: Well answered with the majority using their graph to find the time difference. A small number correctly used their time calculations. Answers: (a) 32 (b)(i) 1415 (ii) 20 (iii) Correct lines drawn (c)(i) 1 hour 20 mins
notes.3c: (i) As part (a) with common errors being 20÷12x100, 1 hour 33, 1 hour 30 and 15/20.
notes.3cii: Again well answered with follow through applied.
notes.4: This proved to be a difficult question for many candidates with some confusion over definitions of mean/ mode/median but more often incorrect misinterpretation of the data provided.
notes.4a: Generally correct interpretation of the given bar chart.
notes.4b: (i) Those candidates who identified the correct row to total to find the number of goals were usually successful. However a significant common error was 36 coming from the total of the first row “number of goals per game”.
notes.4bii: Although the majority of candidates knew the correct method to calculate the mean a lot of errors were seen, including the use of an incorrect value from (i), division by 9, 4 or 36. The use of a “common sense” approach to check this answer would have allowed the candidates to discount a number of incorrect and unrealistic answers.
notes.4iii: Again the method of calculating the median was often recognised with an ordered list commonly seen. However this was often incomplete with, say, 9 values shown.
notes.4iv: This part was poorly answered and the lack of need to show working made it difficult to analyse the problem. Common errors were 8, 20 and 0.
notes.4cii: Completing the pie chart was well answered although a significant number of candidates were unable to attempt this part.
notes.4dii: Also well answered although a common error was 5/40. Answers: (a) 7,8,6,7,5,4; 0,8,12,21,20,20 (b) (i) 103 (ii) 2.575 (iii) 2 (iv) 1
notes.5a: (i) Despite the help given in the wording of the question many candidates were unable to correctly apply a trigonometrical method to solve this part. The setting up of a right-angled triangle and the subsequent use of 40° was not recognised. However those candidates who did so were generally successful.
notes.5aii: Generally well answered on a follow through basis although a common error was applying 12 x10.
notes.5b: Many found it difficult to set up the required linear equation involving the perimeter, with x +x + 2=38, x + 2=38 being the common errors. Those who set up an equation were usually able to earn 1 method mark by showing a correct first step in their algebraic manipulation. Answers: (a) (i) 6.43 (ii) 77.16 (b) 8.5
notes.6a: (i) This part was very well answered.
notes.6aii: Many candidates gave the answer of 8 through a variety of methods; those who did not, often showed no method at all. The clear use of 360÷45 from “number sides= 360÷ size of exterior triangle” was rarely seen.
notes.6iii: This was generally well answered with a follow through applicable.
notes.6b: Many candidates were able to score well in this part showing good knowledge of the required geometric theorems. However all expected common errors resulting from the incorrect use of 360, 180 and 90 were seen. Answers: (a) (i) 45 (ii) 8 (iii) octagon (b) x=90 y=26 z=116
notes.7: A significant number of candidates were able to score well on this question although it was noted that a number were unable to attempt part or all of this question.
notes.7a: Point F was generally positioned correctly although a significant number omitted the construction arcs thereby losing one of the available marks.
notes.7b: The perpendicular bisector was generally positioned correctly although a significant number were inaccurately constructed.
notes.7c: The angle bisector was less well done and a number of construction arcs were difficult to identify.
notes.7d: (i) Although L and M were not always correctly positioned, a follow through basis allowed the majority of candidates to achieve this mark.
notes.7dii: Again the majority were able to score this mark on a follow through basis.
notes.7e: Correct follow through area calculated (f) Correct construction and labelling drawn
notes.7f: This part was the least successful of the entire question with many candidates leaving it blank. The recognition of the correct locus to draw caused problems and those who did draw an arc centred on D often used the wrong radius. Answers: (a) (b) (c) correct construction drawn (d) (i) 6.8-7.3 (ii) 136-146
notes.8a: Very well answered with all values generally correct.
notes.8b: Generally the plotting of these points was good, although errors were often made in plotting (18,1) (-18,-1) and (-3,-6). Two smooth correct curves were generally seen, although as in previous years, common errors included a series of straight lines, “thick” lines, “bumpy” curves or loops. Most candidates knew the required shape and did not draw across the y-axis.
notes.8c: Generally correct although the common errors of 0, 1,180° and “reflection” were seen.
notes.8d: Many correct graphs seen and the points of intersection were usually correct following through from their graph. However a significant number of candidates omitted this part.
notes.8e: Many candidates omitted this part. Some reflections of the curve were seen, with others reflecting just the first quadrant section. Answers: (a) -1,-2,-3,3,2,1 (b) Correct graphs drawn (c) 2 (d) (i) y=x ruled
notes.9a: (i) Generally well answered although the like terms were not always correctly collected together.
notes.9aii: More problems were caused in this part with the term in y often incorrect.
notes.9b: (i) This part was generally answered well.
notes.9bii: More problems in this part with the expansion proving difficult, particularly in the first part. Answers: (a) (i) 3k + 4p – 7 (ii) x-2y² (b) (i) 12 + 21g (ii) 25m³ - 5mt²
notes.10a: (i) Most candidates applied Pythagoras correctly; however answers of 9.4 were common, thereby losing the accuracy mark.
notes.10aii: The use of trigonometry was generally recognised. Those candidates who used the tangent ratio directly with the data given in the question tended to be more successful. Weaker candidates often assumed the angle to be 45°.
notes.10b: (i) Although the correct answer of ‘similar’ was often seen, common errors included ‘congruent’ and ‘proportional’.
notes.10bii: The majority recognised this as an enlargement but often failed to give the full description with the centre often omitted or given as the origin.
notes.10c: This was well answered by the vast majority.
notes.10dii: This part seemed to be more successfully answered than in previous years, although common errors were n+2 and 47.
notes.10e: Many correct answers were seen here often from a pattern continuation. The common errors resulted from using 2 x 47 + 1 instead of solving 2n + 1 = 47 for example. Answers: (a) (i) 9.43 (ii) 32.0 (b) (i) Similar (ii) Enlargement, SF=2, centre A (c) 9,11
notes.general_comments:
The paper gave candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge and application of Mathematics.
Most candidates were able to complete the paper in the allotted time, but there were some candidates who
omitted part or whole questions. The standard of presentation was generally good, however there were
occasions when candidates did not score as they did not show clear working. Centres should continue to
encourage candidates to show formulas used, substitutions made and calculations performed. Attention
should be paid to the degree of accuracy required in each question.
On construction questions candidates should clearly show all construction lines and arcs. Centres should
also continue to encourage candidates to show clear working in the answer space provided.
